title: Collapse five years of history into one starting commit
summary: An imported repository has thousands of irrelevant commits before the part anyone cares about. Truncate the history to a single synthetic root, keeping every file — and understand what you are giving up.
mental_model: History is a chain of parents. To truncate it you build a new root commit holding the tree at your chosen cut-off, then replay everything after it onto that root. The files are identical; everything before the cut simply stops existing.
danger: Truncation destroys blame, bisect and `log -S` for everything before the cut. Once the old objects are pruned, no command can answer 'why is this line here' about them again.

write.content:
# imported from subversion in 2019
OLD = True

setup.run: sh -c 'for i in $(seq 1 12); do printf "# churn %d\n" $i >> legacy.py; git commit -q -a -m "Legacy churn commit $i"; done'
git tag -a rewrite-start -m "Where the interesting history begins"

steps.title: Measure what you are carrying
steps.why: Sixteen commits, thirteen of which are churn from an import nobody has read since. Count them before deciding — truncation is rarely worth it unless the ratio is stark.
steps.expect: Sixteen commits, of which three are the part that matters.

steps.title: Back up before touching anything
steps.why: A branch on the current tip costs nothing and makes every step below reversible. For a truncation, also keep a full clone somewhere — this is the one rewrite you genuinely cannot undo after gc.
steps.expect: A mirror clone holding all sixteen commits, kept as the archive.

verify.label: the full history is archived elsewhere

steps.title: Build a synthetic root commit
steps.why: `commit-tree` with no `-p` makes a parentless commit holding a tree you choose. Here that tree is the cut-off point, so the new root contains every file exactly as it was then.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit-tree rewrite-start^{tree} -m "Truncated history: everything before this is archived separately." > .git/new-root'

steps.expect: A commit with a tree and NO parent line — a second root.

verify.label: the synthetic commit has no parent — it is a root

steps.title: Replay the modern history onto it
steps.why: `rebase --onto <new-root> rewrite-start main` moves the commits after the cut-off onto the new root. The commits before it are simply not in the range, so they are left behind.
steps.expect: Three commits — the synthetic root plus the two that came after the cut-off — and every file still present.

verify.label: history is truncated to three commits

steps.title: Prove the tree is byte-for-byte unchanged
steps.why: The whole promise of a truncation is that the code is identical and only the history is shorter. Diff against the backup branch: an empty result is the proof.
commands: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse main^{tree})" = "$(git rev-parse pre-truncate-backup^{tree})" && echo identical trees'

verify.label: the working tree is identical to before the truncation

steps.title: See exactly what you lost
steps.why: Blame on a legacy line now points at the synthetic root, and `log -S` cannot find when the churn arrived. This is the cost, and it is worth seeing before you make it permanent.
commands: sh -c 'cd ../full-history-archive.git && git log --oneline main -- legacy.py | wc -l'
steps.expect: One commit for legacy.py locally against thirteen in the archive, and the pickaxe now blames the synthetic root for lines written years ago.

verify.label: the legacy file's history collapsed to the synthetic root
…while the archive still has all thirteen commits, which is why you made one

steps.title: Drop the old objects and record what happened
steps.why: Until the backup branch and reflog are gone, nothing has actually shrunk. Delete them, gc, and commit a note explaining where the real history lives — otherwise the next person assumes the project started last Tuesday.

write.content:
# History

Commits before the root of this repository were truncated during an import
cleanup. The full pre-truncation history is archived as a mirror clone and
is available on request — blame and bisect before the root must be run there.

verify.label: the truncation is documented for future readers
verify.hint: a repository whose history starts abruptly needs a note saying why

verify.label: the final history is four commits
history was truncated to the part that matters
verify.hint: commit-tree a new root, then rebase --onto it

verify.label: the full history is preserved in an archive clone
the repository explains where its earlier history went

pitfalls: Truncation is irreversible once you gc. Take a `--mirror` clone first and keep it somewhere durable, not on the same disk.
Every sha changes, so every clone must be recreated. Coordinate it like a migration, not like a commit.
`git blame` on old lines will point at the synthetic root forever. If your team relies on blame for archaeology, the churn is probably worth keeping.
A shallow clone (`--depth`) gives you a small clone without rewriting anything, and can be deepened later. Try that before truncating for real.
Repository size usually comes from large blobs, not from commit count. Measure with `git count-objects -vH` before assuming truncation will help.
cheatsheet: replay the modern history onto it
